scenes.heading: Evaluating statistical reports
scenes.say: Crime up fifty percent! Average salary over a hundred thousand dollars! Headlines love numbers, but numbers can mislead. Let's learn how to check them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A detective questions a witness before believing them
scenes.science: Question the source, evidence and reasoning behind a statistic
scenes.breaks: A report isn't just true or false — it can be partly right, or right but exaggerated.
scenes.say: A good detective doesn't just believe a witness. Who is telling the story? How do they know? Do they have a reason to bend the truth? Treat a statistical report the same way: question the source, the evidence and the reasoning.

scenes.heading: Four checks for any report
steps: Who collected it? How big a sample?
scenes.say: Run four checks. First, the data: who collected it, and how big and fair was the sample? Second, the graphs. Third, the numbers: which average, and percent of what? Fourth, does the conclusion really follow from the data?

scenes.heading: The truncated axis trick
notes: A looks 3 times as tall as B
scenes.say: Here are the same votes drawn twice. On the left, the axis starts at forty-six, so Party A's bar looks three times as tall as Party B's. On the right, the axis starts at zero, and the bars look almost equal. Fifty-two versus forty-eight is only about eight percent more.
scenes.caption: On the left the axis starts at 46, so A looks 3 times as tall. On the right it starts at 0 and the bars look almost equal. 52% vs 48% is only about 8% more.

scenes.heading: Pictures that grow both ways
scenes.say: Cars went from one hundred to one hundred and fifty, one and a half times as many. But the square was made one and a half times as wide and as tall, so its area is two point two five times as big. Your eye sees the area, so the growth looks bigger than it is.

scenes.heading: Which average?
scenes.question: Salaries ($k): 55, 58, 60, 60, 62, 65, 68, 70, 450. "Average salary over $100k" — fair?
scenes.say: A company claims an average salary over a hundred thousand dollars. The mean is about one hundred and five thousand, so it's technically true. But the median is sixty-two thousand, and eight of the nine workers earn seventy thousand or less. One huge salary drags the mean up, so the claim is misleading.
scenes.caption: Mean ≈ $105.33k, but the median is $62k and 8 of 9 workers earn $70k or less. One huge salary drags the mean up: misleading.

scenes.heading: Points vs per cent
scenes.say: When unemployment goes from four percent to five percent, it's up one percentage point, but that's a twenty-five percent increase. Both are true, and each sounds very different. Always ask: percent of what?

points: Check the sample: size, method, who paid
Check axes start at 0 and scales are even
Median beats mean when there are outliers
Percent of what? Points vs per cent
scenes.say: Quick recap. Check the sample and who paid for it. Check the axes and scales. Use the median when there are outliers. Always ask percent of what. And remember, correlation is not causation. Now try the practice questions!
